clue.text: Excited NUS, eager in icy TV hell, examined here?

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up, so the letters of the words that follow are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Agitated student union members, keen despite a frozen hellish television studio, are being tested here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Excited' turns NUS, EAGER, IN, ICY, TV and HELL, nineteen letters in all, into the two words of the answer. NUS is the UK's National Union of Students.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-running British TV quiz tests teams of students, so contestants are examined on the programme.

clue.text: A swindle and without a contract killer?

indicators.note: used in its old sense of outside, so the word and goes round the pieces before it

parts.note: a con is a swindle or confidence trick

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a cheat working without a written agreement counts as a hired assassin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, not lacking. The surface's hired gun is really a snake that squeezes.
explanation.definitionFit: This big snake kills its prey by constriction, so it is wittily a killer that contracts, squeezing tight.

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase before it is to be spoken and heard, giving a sound-alike

parts.note: a helmsman steering is at the tiller

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a barbarian is in charge, steering the ship.
explanation.walkthrough: AT TILLER, a phrase meaning steering, is spoken to sound like the name of the Hun leader.
explanation.definitionFit: The fifth-century leader of the Huns is the archetypal barbarian invader of the Roman world.

clue.text: It seeks Keats' Hellenic effort with Homer, detailed somehow in 1 14 across's intro

indicators.note: somehow says the words are put together in some unspecified way, so their letters are rearranged

parts.words: It seeks Keats' Hellenic effort with

indicators.note: detailed means with its tail cut off, so the last letter of Homer goes

explanation.surface: A quiz programme's opening question asks about Keats's poem on reading a translation of the Greek epic poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' removes R from HOMER; 'somehow' rearranges IT SEEKS KEATS HELLENIC EFFORT WITH plus HOME into the line from Keats's sonnet On First Looking into Chapman's Homer, the opening of the quiz in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue presents this line from Keats's sonnet about Chapman's translation of Homer as the opening of the student quiz show.

clue.text: Thus journalist slants "Healthy Latin no good in healthy English"

indicators.note: in tells us the Latin word and its companions sit inside the English word

parts.note: hale is an English word for healthy, as in hale and hearty
sana is Latin for healthy, as in mens sana in corpore sano

explanation.surface: A headline-writer spins a story about Latin and English words for health.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin feminine for healthy is familiar from the motto mens sana in corpore sano.
explanation.definitionFit: A journalist with a slant or particular viewpoint on a story is said to have one, so the phrase describes slanting.

clue.text: College getting good deal from linguist

parts.note: Poly is short for polytechnic, a British kind of college
a lot means a deal, as in a great deal

explanation.surface: A college gets a generous amount out of a language expert.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who speaks many languages is a linguist in the everyday sense.

clue.text: Drink and drug I take regularly

parts.note: pot is slang for cannabis
to be on a medicine is to take it regularly

explanation.surface: A warning about mixing alcohol with medication that one takes every day.
explanation.definitionFit: A potion is a drink, especially a medicinal or magical one.

clue.text: Garbo's role cut during allied retreat

indicators.note: during says one piece occurs within the span of the other, so it goes inside
retreat means go back, so the synonym for allied is read backwards

parts.note: akin means related or allied
a notch is a small cut

explanation.surface: A film star's part is trimmed while the Allied armies fall back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retreat' reverses the word for allied, and 'during' places the cut inside it. Ninotchka was Garbo's 1939 comedy, billed 'Garbo laughs!'
explanation.definitionFit: Greta Garbo played the title part of the Soviet envoy in the 1939 comedy of this name.

clue.text: Old settlers died with oil pollution

parts.note: ob, from Latin obiit, is the abbreviation for died seen on gravestones

indicators.note: pollution spoils or corrupts the word oil, so its letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Early colonists perished alongside an oil spill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pollution' scrambles OIL. The 'settlers' are not colonists but coins that settle a bill.
explanation.definitionFit: These were small coins of ancient Greece, used to settle debts, so they were old payers of bills.

clue.text: Clubs carried by wild native of the Isle of Wight

indicators.note: carried by means held within, so the clubs letter sits inside the other piece
wild means out of control, so the letters of native run riot

parts.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: A wild islander is seen carrying golf clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' turns NATIVE into VETIAN, and C goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective comes from Vectis, the Roman name for the Isle of Wight, so it means belonging to that island.

clue.text: When do you want amenity management?

indicators.note: management means handling and arranging, so the letters of amenity are reorganised

explanation.surface: A receptionist asks when a guest would like to use the hotel's facilities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'management' rearranges AMENITY. The answer is the reply to the question, which stands in for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The reply means at whatever time you like, the natural answer to a question about preferred timing.

clue.text: Andorra's finalists leave for recreation town in Andalusia

indicators.note: read as re-creation, making the remaining letters into something new
the finalists are the closing letters, and they leave, so the last two letters go

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Andorran athletes who reached the final head off to a Spanish resort for some leisure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finalists leave' drops RA from ANDORRA, leaving ANDOR, and 'for recreation' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: This hilltop town in southern Spain, famous for its gorge and bullring, lies in the region of Andalusia.

clue.text: Church primate left nowt dodgy in this part of Leeds

parts.note: an ape is a primate

indicators.note: dodgy means shifty or unreliable, so the letters of nowt are shifted about

explanation.surface: A clergyman-ape abandons nothing suspicious in a district of a Yorkshire city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dodgy' rearranges NOWT, northern English dialect for nothing, into TOWN.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a district of Leeds in West Yorkshire, just north of the city centre.

parts.note: reads as a break from smoothing clothes, since ironing makes fabric flat and level, but means a free night

explanation.surface: Someone longs for a break from pressing the laundry.
explanation.walkthrough: Ironing evens out creases, so the work could be called evening; a night off it is time out.
explanation.definitionFit: A night when one is free of duties is time out, and ironing is the work of making cloth smooth.

clue.text: No old artisan legion hit trouble with Romans' road direction

indicators.note: to hit trouble is to fall into disarray, so the letters are put in a new order
no here means without, so the letter for old is taken away

explanation.surface: A legion of craftsmen, minus the veterans, runs into difficulties building a Roman road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No old' removes O from LEGION; 'trouble' then rearranges ARTISAN, LEGIN and HIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman roads were famously laid out dead straight, so this phrase describes the course they took.

definitions.meaning: wearing a uniform or official costume, like a servant
belonging to one of the City of London livery companies, the old trade guilds

explanation.surface: Someone has dressed up to entertain guests.
explanation.walkthrough: London's livery companies are ancient trade guilds; a freeman admitted to full membership of one is said to be taken into its livery.
explanation.definitionFit: Servants and guild members wear distinctive uniform, and guild membership is also called the livery.

clue.text: Old solvers' Everest trip in the recent past

parts.note: ye is the old plural you, addressing those doing the puzzle

indicators.note: a trip is a stumble, so the letters of Everest tumble into a new order

explanation.surface: Puzzle-doers of old made an expedition to the world's highest mountain not long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trip' rearranges EVEREST into STEREVE.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic word means yesterday evening, a time in the recent past.

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so the word for scholars runs upwards

parts.note: pupils are scholars or schoolchildren

explanation.surface: Schoolchildren purchased a grammatical error.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'up' turns PUPILS upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A solecism is a mistake in grammar or manners, a blunder.

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the synonym is dropped

parts.note: to fill a space is to occupy it
thy is the archaic form of your

explanation.surface: Someone almost takes over a former military rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts FILL to FIL. 'rank' is the adjective meaning foul, not a military grade.
explanation.definitionFit: Rank as an adjective means foul or disgusting, so it is a synonym.

indicators.note: out of here says the first word stands outside the second, wrapping it

parts.note: set is a synonym of laid, as in the table was laid
the nick is British slang for prison

explanation.surface: An escape route is constructed leading out of a jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' says the word for laid sits outside the prison. A snicket is a northern English word for a narrow alley.
explanation.definitionFit: In northern English dialect this word means a narrow passage or alley between buildings.

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Leftovers from a frenzied, elderly vegan.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across manic, old and vegan.
explanation.definitionFit: Cold vegetables are what is left over from a meal, the leavings.

parts.note: plays on 'right up his street', meaning ideal for him, and a plot named after a London street

explanation.surface: A plot that suits a certain plotter perfectly.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cato Street Conspiracy of 1820 was a plot to murder the British cabinet, named after the London street where the plotters met.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman statesman shares his name with Cato Street, home to an 1820 plot, so the plot is literally his street.

parts.note: a mo, short for moment, is a short term of time
use means employment, as in putting something to use

explanation.surface: A computer worker is on a temporary contract.
explanation.walkthrough: The device that operates a computer is the definition, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: The hand-held pointing device is what a user operates a computer with.
